Title: Truth, Post-Truth, and Technology | Ella McPherson
Source/Citation: McPherson, Ella. Truth, Post-Truth, and Technology. YouTube video, 3 March 2021.
Theme: Digital Rights & Technology; Education & Knowledge Justice; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: The video explores how emerging technologies are reshaping human rights fact-finding, particularly the challenges of verifying information in an environment of misinformation and manipulated content. It considers the opportunities and limitations of technological verification tools, while raising broader questions about efficiency, trust in established information sources, and the role of technology in documenting human rights abuses.

Title: Post-Election 2024: The Future of Human Rights in the U.S.
Source/Citation: Carr Center for Human Rights Policy. “Post-Election 2024: The Future of Human Rights in the U.S.” Harvard Kennedy School, 25 November 2024.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Democracy & Political Power; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: This collection brings together expert perspectives on the implications of the 2024 U.S. presidential election for human rights, including democracy, migration, racial and gender equality, climate justice, and digital rights. Contributors examine potential challenges to existing protections while considering responses through grassroots mobilisation, civil society advocacy, international solidarity, and longer-term efforts to strengthen democratic institutions and human rights.

Title: Rereading the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: Plurality and Contestation, Not Consensus
Source/Citation: Hoover, Joe. “Rereading the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: Plurality and Contestation, Not Consensus.” Journal of Human Rights 12, no. 2 (2013): 217–241.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Global Governance & International Law; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: The article revisits the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, challenging accounts that portray its origins as either a universal consensus or an imposition of liberal Western values. It argues that the Declaration contains an ambiguous understanding of rights that resists both interpretations. Recognising this ambiguity opens possibilities for understanding human rights as an ongoing political struggle over legitimate authority and the meaning of humanity.

Title: Acknowledging the Past in the Post-Truth Era: Witch-Hunts, Lawfare and the Veterans' Amnesty in Northern Ireland
Source/Citation: McEvoy, Kieran. “Acknowledging the Past in the Post-Truth Era: Witch-Hunts, Lawfare and the Veterans’ Amnesty in Northern Ireland.” Journal of Law and Society 53, no. S1 (2026): S42–S55.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Democracy & Political Power; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: The article examines how the British government used narratives of “witch-hunts” and “lawfare” to justify an amnesty for military veterans who served in Northern Ireland. Through this case study, McEvoy explores how post-truth political discourse can undermine efforts to investigate historical wrongdoing, challenging established assumptions about the relationship between law, truth, and accountability in transitional justice.

Title: Social Relations in Commoning: Towards a Socially Innovative Perspective to Action Research in Building Landed Commons
Source/Citation: Moulaert, Frank, Liana Simmons, and Constanza Parra. “Social Relations in Commoning: Towards a Socially Innovative Perspective to Action Research in Building Landed Commons.” In From Land Ownership to Landed Commons: Social Innovation in the Commoning of Scarce Land Resources, 130–157. Edward Elgar Publishing, 2024.
Theme: Economic & Development Justice; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: The chapter examines how social relationships and individual and collective behaviour influence the creation, development, and decline of shared land resources. It highlights the importance of freedom and solidarity in building cooperative relationships and developing forms of governance that can resist unequal power structures. It also considers how these insights can inform action research on commons and their governance.

Title: Politicisation of Human Rights: Current Battlegrounds and Sites of Contestation
Source/Citation: Freedman, R. (2024) Politicisation of human rights: current battlegrounds and sites of contestation. University of Western Australia Law Review, 51 (1). pp. 1-22. ISSN 0042-0328
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Democracy & Political Power; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: The article examines how states and political alliances use different discourses and strategies to challenge the universality of human rights. Drawing on case studies from the UN Human Rights Council, it explores how political actors contest international human rights standards and sometimes use human rights language itself to weaken the international human rights system.

Title: Evangelicals and Human Rights: The Continuing Ambivalence of Evangelical Christians' Support for Human Rights
Source/Citation: Nichols, Joel A. “Evangelicals and Human Rights: The Continuing Ambivalence of Evangelical Christians' Support for Human Rights.” Journal of Law and Religion 24, no. 2 (2008–2009): 629–662.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: The article examines the complex relationship between American evangelical Christianity and international human rights. It argues that evangelical beliefs have encouraged engagement with certain human rights issues, particularly religious freedom, while theological priorities such as evangelism and individual salvation have limited broader support for human rights. Nichols also considers how growing involvement in humanitarian organisations and greater emphasis on human dignity might encourage closer engagement with the human rights movement.

Title: Reparations for Caribbean Slavery and the Potential Impact on Human Well-Being
Source/Citation: Beckles H, Chitre S, Richardson ET. Reparations for Caribbean slavery and the potential impact on human well-being. BMJ Global Health. 2026;11:e017217.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Economic & Development Justice
Key Takeaway: The article examines how the legacies of slavery and colonialism continue to affect health, development, and environmental conditions in the Caribbean, increasing the region's vulnerability to climate change. It presents the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission's Ten-Point Action Plan as a framework for addressing historical injustices through measures such as debt cancellation, public health investment, and cultural preservation, while also responding to present inequalities and future environmental challenges.

Title: Liars, Skeptics, Cheerleaders: Human Rights Implications of Post-Truth Disinformation from State Officials and Politicians
Source/Citation: Deluggi, Nicky, and Cameran Ashraf. “Liars, Skeptics, Cheerleaders: Human Rights Implications of Post-Truth Disinformation from State Officials and Politicians.” Human Rights Review 24 (2023): 365–387.
Theme: Digital Rights & Technology; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: The article examines how deliberate misinformation spread by politicians and state officials can undermine access to information, political participation, and public trust. Drawing on European human rights case law, it considers whether existing legal protections could support a right to truthful information from political leaders. It also argues that human rights law needs a broader understanding of harm to address the long-term effects of political disinformation on individuals and democratic debate.

Title: Human Rights at Risk: Global Governance, American Power, and the Future of Dignity
Source/Citation: Regilme, Salvador Santino F., Jr., and Irene Hadiprayitno, eds. Human Rights at Risk: Global Governance, American Power, and the Future of Dignity. Rutgers University Press, 2022.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Global Governance & International Law; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: The edited volume brings together interdisciplinary perspectives on the challenges facing the international human rights system, including institutional weaknesses, political contestation, authoritarianism, and inequalities in global governance. Through different case studies, contributors examine gaps between human rights commitments and their implementation, as well as the influence of powerful states on human rights protection. The book also considers possible approaches to strengthening international human rights institutions and safeguarding human dignity.

Title: Our Water Commons: Toward a New Freshwater Narrative
Source/Citation: Barlow, Maude. Our Water Commons: Toward a New Freshwater Narrative. Council of Canadians / On the Commons, 2008.
Theme: Climate & Environmental Justice; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Economic & Development Justice
Key Takeaway: The report challenges the treatment of freshwater as a commodity to be bought and sold, arguing instead that water should be protected as a shared resource essential to both human communities and nature. It proposes an alternative approach to water governance based on ecological protection, community participation, public responsibility, and the human right to water. Barlow advocates stronger legal protections and greater local control over water resources to promote equitable and sustainable access.

Title: Human Dignity in International Law
Source/Citation: Le Moli, Ginevra. Human Dignity in International Law. Cambridge University Press, 2021.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: The book traces how human dignity developed into a central principle of international law, examining the historical and philosophical ideas that shaped its recognition. Drawing on legal documents and international judicial decisions, it explores how dignity is understood and applied across international human rights law, humanitarian law, and international criminal law. It offers a historical and legal account of how the concept has evolved within the international legal system.

Title: Truth and Post-Truth in Public Policy: Interpreting the Arguments
Source/Citation: Fischer, Frank. Truth and Post-Truth in Public Policy: Interpreting the Arguments. Elements in Public Policy. Cambridge University Press, 2021.
Theme: Digital Rights & Technology; Democracy & Political Power; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: The book examines why providing more factual information is often insufficient to counter post-truth politics. Fischer argues that understanding misinformation and political disagreement also requires attention to how people interpret facts through social meanings, emotions, and political beliefs. Using debates about climate change and COVID-19, he develops an interpretive approach to policy analysis that examines how competing narratives shape public understanding and responses to scientific evidence.

Title: The Cambridge Handbook of Human Dignity: Interdisciplinary Perspectives
Source/Citation: Düwell, Marcus, Jens Braarvig, Roger Brownsword, and Dietmar Mieth, eds. The Cambridge Handbook of Human Dignity: Interdisciplinary Perspectives. Cambridge University Press, 2014.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Faith & Freedom of Religion; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: This interdisciplinary collection explores how human dignity has been understood across different historical periods, cultures, religious traditions, and philosophical approaches. It examines both European and non-Western perspectives, considers the relationship between dignity and human rights, and investigates how dignity is interpreted in law, justice, medicine, and other fields. The volume provides multiple perspectives for understanding the foundations, meanings, and practical applications of human dignity.

Title: Wilding at Mozilla Festival 2026
Source/Citation: Abi Assy, Zeina. “Wilding at Mozilla Festival 2026.” Mozilla Foundation, 2026.
Theme: Digital Rights & Technology; Human Rights Futures & Theory; Climate & Environmental Justice
Key Takeaway: Drawing inspiration from ecological regeneration and personal experiences of land and community in Lebanon, the essay proposes a different vision for technology: one based on openness, collective ownership, and mutual care rather than centralised control and extraction. It highlights community-led initiatives, including independent digital networks, open-source tools, and anti-surveillance technologies, as examples of how technology can support more diverse, resilient, and equitable futures.

Title: Decolonising Human Rights
Source/Citation: Shetty, Salil. “Decolonising Human Rights.” Speech delivered at the London School of Economics, 22 May 2018. Amnesty International.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: The speech argues that decolonising human rights requires reconnecting the international human rights movement with ordinary people's struggles against abuses of power. Shetty examines how governments, powerful states, and international organisations have used or controlled human rights for their own interests, often weakening the influence of affected communities. He calls for greater grassroots leadership, stronger connections between political and socioeconomic rights, and renewed attention to emerging challenges posed by corporate power and technology.

Title: Copenhagen Decolonization Collective
Source/Citation: Copenhagen Decolonization Collective, formerly Decolonizing Global Health
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice; Economic & Development Justice
Key Takeaway: A volunteer-run, student-led initiative that grew beyond global health to examine colonial power across institutions, knowledge systems and everyday life. It offers a decolonisation library, toolkit, reading course and blog to support collective learning and the imagining of decolonial futures.

Title: Decolonial Futures
Source/Citation: History, Memory and Decolonial Futures Research Collective. Decolonial Futures [Podcast series]. University of Melbourne, 2026.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Human Rights Futures & Theory; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: The podcast brings together researchers, artists, and creative practitioners to explore how colonial histories continue to shape contemporary societies and how alternative futures might be imagined. Through conversations connecting scholarship and creative practice, it examines approaches to challenging colonial power, rethinking dominant narratives, and creating space for different perspectives and ways of understanding the world.

Title: Decolonization in Action
Source/Citation: Bonhomme, Edna, and Kristyna Comer. Decolonization in Action [Podcast series]. 2019–2021.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Accountability & Reparations
Key Takeaway: The podcast explores how colonial histories and structures continue to influence contemporary societies and how people challenge these legacies through activism, scholarship, and cultural practices. Featuring conversations on subjects such as reparations, restitution, and knowledge production, it connects decolonial ideas with practical struggles for change and highlights different approaches to confronting historical and continuing inequalities.

Title: In Earth's Care
Source/Citation: Gesturing Towards Decolonial Futures Collective. In Earth’s Care [Podcast series]. 2022.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Climate & Environmental Justice; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: This podcast series brings together different voices and perspectives to explore relationships between people, communities, and the Earth. Engaging with Indigenous knowledge, colonial histories, and ecological challenges, it encourages reflection on how dominant approaches to development and sustainability might be reconsidered. The series invites listeners to imagine more responsible and reciprocal ways of relating to one another and the natural world.

Title: Te Āo Māori “Accountability”: Indigenous Ways Toward Partnership and Restorative Practice Globally
Source/Citation: Rawson-Te Patu, Emma. “Te Āo Māori ‘Accountability’: Indigenous Ways Toward Partnership and Restorative Practice Globally.” Health and Human Rights Journal 27, no. 2 (2025): 21–22.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Explores accountability through a Māori worldview, arguing that justice should prioritise relationships, reciprocity, healing and partnership rather than punishment. Suggests Indigenous approaches offer a model for reimagining human rights accountability and co-creating more equitable futures.

Title: World Cup: Rethinking Human Rights Strategy
Source/Citation: Coombes, Thomas, and Osama Bhutta. “World Cup: Rethinking Human Rights Strategy.” Hope-Based Communications, 11 June 2026.
Theme: Grassroots Movements & Participation; Human Rights Futures & Theory; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: Drawing on human rights campaigning around the Qatar World Cup, this conversation questions whether international criticism and public shaming effectively change attitudes or improve conditions for affected communities. Coombes and Bhutta explore alternative strategies based on locally relevant values, storytelling, intercultural dialogue, and opportunities for meaningful action. They argue that human rights organisations should combine accountability with approaches that build trust, recognise progress, and engage communities as participants in change.

Title: Leak Exposes Members of Peter Thiel’s Secretive ‘Dialog’ Society
Source/Citation: Cameron, Dell, and Yulia Almazova. “Leak Exposes Members of Peter Thiel’s Secretive ‘Dialog’ Society.” WIRED, June 2026.
Theme: Digital Rights & Technology; Democracy & Political Power; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: This investigation examines Dialog, a private network connecting influential figures from technology, business, and government. Drawing on exposed internal records, it reveals the network's membership, confidential gatherings, and discussions about artificial intelligence, security, and societal change. The reporting raises questions about transparency and the concentration of influence in spaces where powerful actors exchange ideas about emerging technologies and possible futures, often away from public scrutiny.

Title: Human Rights Ecosystem: From Ideas to Action
Source/Citation: Videre Est Credere. Human Rights Ecosystem: From Ideas to Action. 2026.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: This strategy note calls for transforming a fragmented human rights sector by shifting power toward affected communities and strengthening collaboration between organisations. It questions approaches that prioritise collecting evidence for distant international mechanisms without ensuring meaningful redress. Videre proposes four practical steps: assessing AI's implications for human rights defenders, establishing shared support services, improving coordination around evidence, and developing stronger rapid-response systems to support locally led accountability.

Title: Nick Estes: The Future Must Be Socialist
Source/Citation: Progressive International. “Nick Estes: The Future Must Be Socialist.” Video featuring Nick Estes, 2020. YouTube.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Climate & Environmental Justice; Economic & Development Justice
Key Takeaway: Nick Estes presents an Indigenous-informed vision of ecological and social justice that places the well-being of the Earth alongside human relationships. He criticises capitalist overconsumption and the displacement of Indigenous peoples from their lands, arguing that environmental protection requires restoring Indigenous stewardship and establishing more equitable social relations. Estes advocates socialism as a necessary alternative for achieving an ecologically sustainable future.

Title: Britain: The F* Word and a GOOD BYE to Democracy
Source/Citation: Decolonial Dispatch. “Britain: The F* Word and a GOOD BYE to Democracy.” Featuring Luke de Noronha, 8 October 2025. Podcast episode, 51 minutes.
Theme: Democracy & Political Power; Migration & Displacement; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: This episode features Luke de Noronha in a discussion about the growing influence of far-right politics in Britain and its implications for democracy, migration, and public debate. It examines how exclusionary political narratives can become increasingly accepted and considers the challenges facing those seeking to resist them. The conversation also raises questions about the political consequences of pessimistic visions of the future and the need to develop alternative narratives.

Title: Does the World Need New Leaders? Varsha Gandikota & Naledi Pandor | Reframe
Source/Citation: Al Jazeera English. “Does the World Need New Leaders? Varsha Gandikota & Naledi Pandor.” Reframe, 19 April 2026. Video interview.
Theme: Global Governance & International Law; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: In this interview, former South African Foreign Minister Naledi Pandor reflects on the unequal distribution of power in international politics and the need for stronger international solidarity. Drawing on South Africa's anti-apartheid struggle and its legal action concerning Gaza, she discusses the limitations of existing international institutions, the effects of Islamophobia, and the importance of principled political leadership. She also emphasises organised collective action, diplomatic cooperation, and greater participation by Global South countries in shaping international affairs.

Title: The Politics of Human Rights
Source/Citation: Gready, Paul. “The Politics of Human Rights.” Third World Quarterly 24, no. 4 (2003): 745–757.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: The article challenges the tendency to view politics mainly as a source of corruption or manipulation in human rights. While recognising how powerful economic and political actors can use human rights to advance their interests, Gready argues that rights can also enable resistance, collective action, and social transformation. He proposes a more constructive understanding of human rights politics that acknowledges unequal power while preserving opportunities for political agency, contestation, and change.

Title: Authoritarian Legacies in Law and Democratic Backsliding: The Case of Turkey’s Specially Authorized Courts
Source/Citation: Över, Defne. “Authoritarian Legacies in Law and Democratic Backsliding: The Case of Turkey’s Specially Authorized Courts.” Law & Social Inquiry 51, no. 1 (2026): 203–230. Published online 1 September 2025.
Theme: Democracy & Political Power; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Examining Türkiye's Specially Authorized Courts, the article explores how governments can exploit authoritarian features inherited from earlier legal systems to weaken democratic institutions. Över argues that the AKP government used these courts to constrain political opponents while presenting institutional reforms and legal proceedings as steps toward democratisation. The study shows how authoritarian legal legacies can serve both to exercise political power and to legitimise democratic backsliding.

Title: Judicial Transformation in a Competitive Authoritarian Regime: Evidence from the Turkish Case
Source/Citation: Esen, Berk. “Judicial Transformation in a Competitive Authoritarian Regime: Evidence from the Turkish Case.” Law & Policy 47, no. 1 (2025): e12250.
Theme: Democracy & Political Power; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: The article examines how weaknesses in Türkiye's judicial system contributed to democratic backsliding. Esen argues that the political involvement of courts aligned with the secular establishment allowed the AKP government to portray judicial reforms as necessary for democracy, while gradually increasing its control over the judiciary. The study shows how conflicts between courts and elected governments can be used to justify institutional changes that ultimately weaken judicial independence and democratic accountability.

Title: The Role of the Opposition in Autocratisation: The Case of Turkey
Source/Citation: Korkmaz, Seren Selvin. “The Role of the Opposition in Autocratisation: The Case of Turkey.” Third World Quarterly (2024): 258–275.
Theme: Democracy & Political Power; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: Examining Türkiye's main opposition party between 2002 and 2022, Korkmaz explores how opposition strategies can influence democratic backsliding. She distinguishes between rigid opposition, characterised by identity-based polarisation, and flexible opposition, involving broader alliances and more inclusive political language. The article argues that although flexibility can help opposition parties respond to growing authoritarianism, it also carries risks, including weakening party identity and potentially reinforcing the political dynamics it seeks to challenge.

Title: Civic Opposition and Democratic Backsliding: Mobilization Dynamics and Rapport with Political Parties
Source/Citation: Yabanci, Bilge. “Civic Opposition and Democratic Backsliding: Mobilization Dynamics and Rapport with Political Parties.” Government and Opposition 60, no. 2 (2025): 431–455.
Theme: Democracy & Political Power; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: The article examines how civil society groups can organise against democratic backsliding, drawing on cases from Türkiye and Hungary. Yabanci develops a framework for understanding resilient civic opposition, focusing on how movements connect different grievances, combine street protests with other forms of mobilisation, and interact with opposition political parties. The study offers a way to assess the conditions that shape civic resistance to growing authoritarianism beyond formal party politics.

Title: Why the Human Rights Movement Needs Hard Conversations Now
Source/Citation: Santos, Lucila. “Why the Human Rights Movement Needs Hard Conversations Now.” OpenGlobalRights, 21 April 2026.
Theme: Grassroots Movements & Participation; Human Rights Futures & Theory; Economic & Development Justice
Key Takeaway: Drawing on discussions convened by the International Network of Civil Liberties Organizations, Santos examines the need to rethink human rights strategies amid political, institutional, and financial pressures. She highlights proposals for strengthening grassroots organising, reducing dependence on international donors, engaging audiences beyond established activist circles, and recognising the political dimensions of human rights advocacy. The article also emphasises creating dedicated space for collective reflection and long-term planning rather than remaining focused exclusively on immediate crises.

Title: Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice on the Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change
Source/Citation: United Nations General Assembly. Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice on the Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change. A/RES/80/263, 20 May 2026.
Theme: Climate & Environmental Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Accountability & Reparations
Key Takeaway: On 20 May 2026, the UN General Assembly voted 141–8 to support the ICJ’s climate advisory opinion, reinforcing the idea that states have legal obligations to address climate change. The US, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Israel, Yemen, Liberia and Belarus opposed it.

Title: Private Power and Democracy’s Decline: How to Make Capitalism Support Democracy
Source/Citation: Kurz, Mordecai. Private Power and Democracy’s Decline: How to Make Capitalism Support Democracy. MIT Press, 2026.
Theme: Democracy & Political Power; Economic & Development Justice; Digital Rights & Technology
Key Takeaway: The book examines how technological innovation and concentrated corporate power can contribute to economic inequality and undermine democracy. Focusing on the United States, Kurz argues that unregulated capitalism allows dominant firms to accumulate lasting market power while exposing workers to economic insecurity. He proposes a more regulated economic system, including policies to protect livelihoods, so that technological progress benefits society more broadly without reinforcing political and economic inequalities.

Title: Building Up Imaginary Enemies: Misinformation, Disinformation and ‘Foreign Agent’ Allegations in President Prabowo’s Indonesia
Source/Citation: Amnesty International. Indonesia: “Building Up Imaginary Enemies”: Misinformation, Disinformation and ‘Foreign Agent’ Allegations in President Prabowo’s Indonesia. ASA 21/0931/2026, 19 May 2026.
Theme: Digital Rights & Technology; Democracy & Political Power; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: The report investigates how coordinated online disinformation campaigns in Indonesia have targeted journalists, activists, and civil society organisations by portraying them as agents of foreign interests. Amnesty International examines the involvement of state-linked actors, the relationship between online attacks and offline intimidation, and the role of social media platforms in amplifying harmful narratives. It highlights how disinformation can undermine freedom of expression, discourage civic participation, and increase risks faced by human rights defenders.

Title: Migration and the European Convention on Human Rights: Legal Requirements, Calls for Reform and Resulting Developments
Source/Citation: Kennedy, Harriet. Migration and the European Convention on Human Rights: Legal Requirements, Calls for Reform and Resulting Developments. European Parliamentary Research Service, 2026.
Theme: Migration & Displacement; Global Governance & International Law; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: This briefing examines growing political pressure to reconsider the application of the European Convention on Human Rights to migration and deportation. It explains the protections provided by Articles 3 and 8, reviews calls for reform, and analyses the Council of Europe's 2026 Chișinău Declaration. It explores tensions between migration-control priorities, individual rights, and judicial independence, while considering how political developments may influence the future interpretation of established human rights protections.

Title: Chișinău Declaration
Source/Citation: Council of Europe, Committee of Ministers. Chișinău Declaration. CM(2026)99-final, adopted 15 May 2026.
Theme: Migration & Displacement; Global Governance & International Law; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: Adopted by the Council of Europe's 46 member states, the Chișinău Declaration addresses how the European Convention on Human Rights should operate in the context of contemporary migration challenges. It reaffirms states' commitment to the Convention and the independence of the European Court of Human Rights, while emphasising national responsibilities for border control and public safety. The declaration addresses protections against ill-treatment, private and family life, and proposals for managing migration within the Convention framework.

Title: Tribal Sufferings: Revisiting the Human Rights Approach from a Global South Perspective with a Special Reference to India
Source/Citation: Mark, Stency Mariya. “Tribal Sufferings: Revisiting the Human Rights Approach from a Global South Perspective with a Special Reference to India.” Economic and Political Weekly 60, no. 4 (2025).
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Climate & Environmental Justice
Key Takeaway: Examines how tribal communities in India have been displaced and marginalised through colonial and neoliberal development models. It questions whether individualistic, market-oriented approaches to rights can adequately address collective injustices. Drawing on Global South critiques of human rights and Nancy Fraser's theory of redistribution and recognition, Mark argues for an approach that protects communal land rights, cultural identities, and collective well-being. The article calls for a more inclusive understanding of development that prioritises communities' rights over purely economic objectives.

Title: Reimagining Human Rights for an Uncertain World
Source/Citation: Nowrojee, Binaifer. “Reimagining Human Rights for an Uncertain World.” Presidential Lecture, Central European University, Vienna, 18 June 2026. Open Society Foundations.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: Nowrojee calls for reimagining human rights beyond defending existing institutions and responding to violations. She argues that human rights must be understood as a universal but plural project, shaped by different traditions and collective struggles rather than dominated by powerful states. Emphasising the limits of legal approaches alone, she advocates renewed political organising, broader coalitions, community leadership, and positive visions of justice that address inequality, technological power, and global uncertainty.

Title: New Advocates and the Future of International Human Rights
Source/Citation: Nowrojee, Binaifer. “New Advocates and the Future of International Human Rights.” Opening remarks, Chatham House, London, 15 June 2026. Open Society Foundations.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Nowrojee argues that the future of international human rights is increasingly being shaped by grassroots movements, younger generations, legal advocates, and states outside traditional centres of global power. Challenging narratives of inevitable decline, she highlights how these actors combine political mobilisation with legal strategies and advocate broader understandings of rights, including economic, collective, and environmental justice. She calls for international institutions and philanthropic organisations to share power and support community-led efforts.

Title: Indigenous Cinema: A New Mode of Creative Self-Determination
Source/Citation: Driver, Tom. “Indigenous Cinema: A New Mode of Creative Self-Determination.” OpenGlobalRights, 23 October 2025.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Education & Knowledge Justice; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: The commentary explores how cinema can become a form of creative self-determination, enabling communities to represent their experiences, knowledge, and relationships with land on their own terms. Through two films by Indigenous creators, it examines how storytelling can challenge colonial narratives, communicate ecological perspectives beyond human-centred approaches, and encourage audiences to reconsider their relationship with nature and Indigenous claims to territorial sovereignty.

Title: Bakish Rao: Plantas en Lucha
Source/Citation: Baniwa, Denilson, and Comando Matico, directors. Bakish Rao: Plantas en Lucha. 2024.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Climate & Environmental Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Created by Indigenous artists from Brazil and Peru, this experimental science-fiction film imagines ecological destruction and resistance from the perspective of plants. Challenging human-centred narratives, it explores the consequences of monoculture and the homogenisation of living environments. Through speculative storytelling, the film invites audiences to consider relationships between human and nonhuman life, offering an alternative way to imagine ecological futures beyond conventional ideas of development and exploitation.

Title: Lithipokoroda
Source/Citation: Baniwa, Lilly, director. Lithipokoroda. 2021.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Education & Knowledge Justice; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: The film uses Indigenous performance and visual storytelling to confront colonial violence, environmental destruction, and the marginalisation of ancestral knowledge. Centred on an ancestral woman's journey through the forest, it explores the relationship between territory, cultural survival, and resistance. By bringing Indigenous voices and creative expression to the foreground, Lithipokoroda presents filmmaking as a way to reclaim narratives and assert cultural self-determination.

Title: Stop Mourning the Old NATO. Build the New One.
Source/Citation: Dalay, Galip. “Stop Mourning the Old NATO. Build the New One.” TIME, 7 July 2026.
Theme: Global Governance & International Law; Democracy & Political Power; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Dalay argues that European security cannot rely indefinitely on NATO's traditional dependence on American leadership. Rather than attempting to restore the previous transatlantic order, he proposes a more adaptable European security architecture that includes non-EU NATO members, engages neighbouring regions, and uses flexible coalitions to address specific challenges. The article invites broader reflection on how established international institutions might adapt when geopolitical relationships and assumptions about global power change.

Title: Neo-democracy: Legal Empowerment and the Reincarnation of Democracy in Africa
Source/Citation: Atuguba, Raymond A. “Neo-democracy: Legal Empowerment and the Reincarnation of Democracy in Africa.” International Journal of Constitutional Law 24, no. 2 (2026): 387–394.
Theme: Democracy & Political Power; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Atuguba challenges the idea that the difficulties facing Western liberal democracy necessarily signal democracy's decline everywhere. Drawing on African constitutional traditions and grassroots legal practices, he proposes a model of democracy centred on legal empowerment: people's ability to understand, use, and shape the law. He argues that democratic renewal requires more than elections and formal institutions, emphasising accessible justice, social welfare, citizen participation, and locally grounded approaches to governance.

Title: Reclaiming Human Rights in a Changing World Order
Source/Citation: Sabatini, Christopher, ed. Reclaiming Human Rights in a Changing World Order. Washington, DC: Brookings Institution Press and Chatham House, 2022.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Global Governance & International Law; Digital Rights & Technology
Key Takeaway: This edited volume examines how geopolitical competition, populism, religious movements, and emerging technologies are challenging international and regional human rights systems. Bringing together scholars and practitioners, it explores threats to established institutions across different regions and proposes ways to strengthen their legitimacy and effectiveness. The book calls for institutional reform, wider participation, and renewed international cooperation, while considering how human rights protections can adapt to a changing global order.

Title: Picturing the Pipeline: Mapping Settler Colonialism on Instagram
Source/Citation: Karsgaard, Carrie, and Maggie MacDonald. “Picturing the Pipeline: Mapping Settler Colonialism on Instagram.” New Media & Society 22, no. 7 (2020): 1206–1226.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Climate & Environmental Justice; Digital Rights & Technology
Key Takeaway: Through Instagram posts about Canada's Trans Mountain pipeline, Karsgaard and MacDonald examine how images and hashtags shape public debates over development, Indigenous sovereignty, and environmental resistance. Their analysis shows how digital representations connect local experiences to national politics, revealing Instagram as a contested space where settler-colonial assumptions can be reproduced, challenged, and potentially transformed.

Title: Indigenous Media and Social Media Convergence: Adaptation of Storytelling on Twitter, SoundCloud and YouTube
Source/Citation: Mpofu, Phillip. “Indigenous Media and Social Media Convergence: Adaptation of Storytelling on Twitter, SoundCloud and YouTube.” Journal of Asian and African Studies 57, no. 6 (2022): 1199–1213.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Digital Rights & Technology; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Far from disappearing in the digital age, Indigenous storytelling traditions in Zimbabwe are finding new forms of expression on Twitter, SoundCloud, and YouTube. Mpofu shows how oral narratives are adapted, shared, and reinvented through social media, creating opportunities for cultural participation and continuity. These practices challenge assumptions that technological change inevitably erodes traditional knowledge, revealing how digital spaces can sustain and transform Indigenous forms of communication.

Title: Indigenous Articulations of Social Media and Digital Assemblages of Care
Source/Citation: Frazer, Ryan, Bronwyn Carlson, and Terri Farrelly. “Indigenous Articulations of Social Media and Digital Assemblages of Care.” Digital Geography and Society 3 (2022): 100038.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Digital Rights & Technology; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: Examining Indigenous Australians' everyday use of social media, the article explores how digital networks enable communities to organise care, safety, and mutual support. Challenging research that treats Indigenous people primarily as recipients of formal health services, the authors show how users actively identify needs and create relationships of assistance through online connections. It presents these practices as alternative spaces of collective well-being that challenge dominant assumptions about Indigenous digital life.

Title: Indigenous Digital Life: The Practice and Politics of Being Indigenous on Social Media
Source/Citation: Carlson, Bronwyn, and Ryan Frazer. Indigenous Digital Life: The Practice and Politics of Being Indigenous on Social Media. Palgrave Macmillan, 2021.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Digital Rights & Technology; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Drawing on several years of research into Indigenous Australians' experiences of social media, Carlson and Frazer challenge colonial representations of Indigenous peoples as belonging to the past. They examine how digital platforms shape identity, community, relationships, and experiences of discrimination, while also creating opportunities for Indigenous agency and creativity. The book presents Indigenous digital life as a future-oriented practice through which communities actively build connections, assert sovereignty, and imagine different social worlds.

Title: Disrupting the Colonial Algorithm: Indigenous Australia and Social Media
Source/Citation: Fredericks, Bronwyn, Abraham Bradfield, Jenny Nguyen, and Samar Ansell. “Disrupting the Colonial Algorithm: Indigenous Australia and Social Media.” Media International Australia 183, no. 1 (2022): 158–178.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Digital Rights & Technology; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Examining Indigenous-led social media campaigns in Australia, the article explores how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities use digital platforms to challenge colonial representations and assert their own perspectives. The authors describe these interventions as disrupting “colonial algorithms” that shape public understandings of Indigenous identities. It highlights how online activism can make continuing injustices visible and create opportunities for Indigenous communities to influence public narratives.

Title: Indigenous Sovereignty in Digital Territory: A Qualitative Study on Land-Based Relations with #NativeTwitter
Source/Citation: Caranto Morford, Ashley, and Jeffrey Ansloos. “Indigenous Sovereignty in Digital Territory: A Qualitative Study on Land-Based Relations with #NativeTwitter.” AlterNative: An International Journal of Indigenous Peoples 17, no. 2 (2021): 293–305.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Digital Rights & Technology; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: The article examines how Indigenous language networks on Twitter sustain relationships with territories, cultures, and communities. The qualitative study identifies digital practices that connect people to homelands, support language revitalisation, and navigate settler colonialism online. It presents Indigenous digital sovereignty as extending beyond technological access to encompass land-based relationships, cultural continuity, and struggles for justice in digital environments.

Title: Why Reparations? Q&A
Source/Citation: Human Rights Watch. “Why Reparations? Q&A.” 19 June 2025.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Focusing on the United States, Human Rights Watch explains how slavery and subsequent racial discrimination continue to affect Black communities. It discusses different forms of repair, including financial payments, public acknowledgment, community investment, and institutional reform. The Q&A also outlines existing reparations initiatives and argues that meaningful solutions should be developed with the communities affected by historical and ongoing injustice.

Title: The Future of Human Rights: From Gatekeeping to Symbiosis
Source/Citation: Rodríguez-Garavito, César. “The Future of Human Rights: From Gatekeeping to Symbiosis.” SUR – International Journal on Human Rights, no. 20 (2014).
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Rodríguez-Garavito argues that the human rights movement needs to become more open, diverse, and collaborative. Rather than allowing large organisations and legal experts to dominate decisions, he proposes a system where grassroots groups, local organisations, activists, and international institutions work together as equal partners. This approach would help the movement respond to changing global power relations, new technologies, and environmental challenges while making better use of different forms of knowledge and experience.

Title: “Unacceptable to Our People”: Diverse Cultural Beliefs, Indigenous Rights, and the Future of Human Activities on the Moon
Source/Citation: Barentine, John C. “‘Unacceptable to Our People’: Diverse Cultural Beliefs, Indigenous Rights, and the Future of Human Activities on th
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Global Governance & International Law; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: As commercial space activities expand, Barentine raises concerns about the exclusion of Indigenous communities whose cultural and spiritual traditions give the Moon special significance. Using disputes over sending human remains to the lunar surface, he questions whether existing space laws adequately respect different cultural perspectives. He calls for Indigenous peoples to help shape future decisions about space, rather than simply being consulted after plans are made.

Title: Orbán’s Danube Institute Quietly Launches a Nonprofit Arm in the United States
Source/Citation: Global Project Against Hate and Extremism. “Orbán’s Danube Institute Quietly Launches a Nonprofit Arm in the United States.” 13 July 2026.
Theme: Democracy & Political Power; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: This investigation examines the Danube Institute's expansion from Hungary into the United States, documenting connections with American conservative organisations and political figures. It raises questions about how these partnerships may help spread political agendas internationally, including positions affecting women's rights, LGBTQ+ protections, and democratic institutions.

Title: The Engine Room’s Futures Podcast
Source/Citation: The Engine Room. “The Futures Podcast.” The Engine Room, 2025–2026.
Theme: Digital Rights & Technology; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Through conversations and personal reflections, The Engine Room's podcast considers how communities can shape technology according to their own needs and values. Episodes connect questions about digital rights and collective care with memories, ancestral knowledge, and relationships with people and places. The series encourages listeners to imagine futures informed not only by technological change, but also by the knowledge communities already hold.

Title: How Emerging Movements Are Redefining Democracy Across Africa
Source/Citation: Eze, Chukwuemeka. “How Emerging Movements Are Redefining Democracy Across Africa.” Open Society Foundations, 5 December 2025.
Theme: Democracy & Political Power; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Across Africa, young people, women, artists, farmers, and community organisers are challenging traditional ideas about who should shape democracy. Eze describes how these groups are creating new forms of political participation and demanding greater accountability, economic justice, and dignity. Inspired by the African philosophy of ubuntu, he presents a vision of democracy based on shared responsibility, collective well-being, and stronger citizen involvement in decisions that shape their futures.

Title: TWAIL Pedagogy: Legal Education for Emancipation
Source/Citation: al Attar, Mohsen and Tava, Vernon Ivan, TWAIL Pedagogy - Legal Education for Emancipation (July 23, 2009). Palestine Yearbook of International Law, Vol. 15, No. 7, 2010.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: This article examines how traditional legal education can reinforce unequal power relations and colonial perspectives in international law. Using an international law course as an example, the authors discuss an alternative teaching approach based on critical thinking, student participation and dialogue. They argue that legal education should encourage students to question established legal structures and consider their implications for global justice.

Title: TWAIL Pedagogy: Teaching International Law Better
Source/Citation: al Attar, Mohsen and Quintero, Rafael, TWAIL Pedagogy: Teaching International Law Better (June 01, 2024), in Antony Anghie et al. TWAIL Reader (Edward Elgar, 2024).
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: International law is often taught without sufficient attention to its colonial history and the inequalities it has helped sustain. Al Attar and Quintero argue that teaching informed by Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL) can provide a more critical understanding of the field. They suggest that recognising international law's historical role in maintaining unequal power relations is necessary for imagining a fairer international legal system.

Title: Beyond the (Post)Colonial: TWAIL and the Everyday Life of International Law
Source/Citation: Eslava, Luis and Pahuja, Sundhya, Beyond the (Post)Colonial: TWAIL and the Everyday Life of International Law (April 4, 2012). Journal of Law and Politics in Africa, Asia and Latin America - Verfassung und Recht in Übersee (VRÜ), Vol. 45(2), 2012, pp. 195-221.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: This article examines how international law shapes everyday life, including through institutions, policies and practices that may reproduce colonial inequalities. Eslava and Pahuja argue that understanding international law requires looking beyond treaties and courts to its effects on people and communities. The article also considers how everyday forms of resistance can challenge existing power relations and contribute to developing a more inclusive international legal order.

Title: When Independence Meets Accountability: Upholding Non-Retrogression in the Human Rights System
Source/Citation: Agosti, Tania, Andrea Baldwin, Susana T. Fried, Jaime M. Gher, Mariah Grant, Alice M. Miller, Mindy Jane Roseman, and Nerima Akinyi Were. “When Independence Meets Accountability: Upholding Non-Retrogression in the Human Rights System.” Health and Human Rights 27, no. 2 (2025): 23–26.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Global Governance & International Law; Gender & Social Justice
Key Takeaway: The authors examine tensions between the independence and accountability of UN human rights experts, particularly in relation to gender equality and gender-based violence. They argue that some recent interpretations risk weakening existing protections for transgender people and sex workers. The article calls for greater transparency, stronger professional standards, and constructive civil society oversight to prevent the erosion of rights while preserving expert independence.

Title: The Sweet Spot Between Formalism and Fairness: Indigenous Peoples’ Contribution to International Law
Source/Citation: Charters, Claire. “The Sweet Spot Between Formalism and Fairness: Indigenous Peoples’ Contribution to International Law.” AJIL Unbound 115 (2021): 123–128.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Indigenous Peoples are contributing to changes in international law by challenging its traditional focus on states and demanding greater recognition of their rights and authority. Charters examines their growing participation in international decision-making and the development of different forms of self-determination. She argues that international law can become more inclusive while retaining binding rules that protect communities against abuses of state power.

Title: Original Nation Approaches to “Inter-National” Law (ONAIL)
Source/Citation: Fukurai, Hiroshi. “Original Nation Approaches to ‘Inter-National’ Law (ONAIL): Decoupling of the Nation and the State and the Search for New Legal Orders.” Indiana Journal of Global Legal Studies 26, no. 1 (2019): 199–262.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Global Governance & International Law; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Fukurai challenges the state-centred foundations of international law and examines how governments and corporations have contributed to the displacement of Indigenous peoples and environmental destruction. He proposes an alternative approach that places Indigenous nations and their rights at the centre of international relations. The article considers how cooperation between communities, new legal institutions, and approaches recognising nature's rights could support self-determination and protect cultural and environmental diversity.

Title: Original Nation Approaches to Inter-National Law
Source/Citation: Fukurai, Hiroshi, and Richard Krooth. Original Nation Approaches to Inter-National Law: The Quest for the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and Nature in the Age of Anthropocene. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan, 2021.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Global Governance & International Law; Climate & Environmental Justice
Key Takeaway: The book challenges international law's traditional focus on states by examining the histories and struggles of Indigenous nations. Fukurai and Krooth argue that existing political and legal systems have contributed to the loss of Indigenous lands, cultural diversity and environmental protection. They propose an alternative approach that places Indigenous self-determination, cooperation between nations and the rights of nature at the centre of a more inclusive international legal order.

Title: Decolonizing the Responsibility to Protect: On Pervasive Eurocentrism, Southern Agency and Struggles over Universals
Source/Citation: Pison Hindawi, Coralie. “Decolonizing the Responsibility to Protect: On Pervasive Eurocentrism, Southern Agency and Struggles over Universals.” Security Dialogue 53, no. 1 (2022): 38–56.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: The Responsibility to Protect is often criticised as a Western concept that can justify intervention in other countries. Pison Hindawi challenges this understanding by highlighting how states from the Global South have also influenced its development. She argues that decolonising international law requires recognising their role in shaping international principles and understanding how different countries negotiate competing ideas about universal rights and responsibilities.

Title: Decolonising International Law: Development, Economic Growth and the Politics of Universality
Source/Citation: Pahuja, Sundhya. Decolonising International Law: Development, Economic Growth and the Politics of Universality. Cambridge Studies in International and Comparative Law 86. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2011.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Economic & Development Justice
Key Takeaway: Pahuja examines how international law has shaped development policies and relations between wealthy and poorer countries. Through examples involving decolonisation, natural resources and foreign investment, she argues that international law's promises of equality have often been redirected towards economic models that preserve existing inequalities. The book questions how ideas presented as universal can reinforce unequal power relations and considers the possibilities for challenging them.

Title: Voice of the Voiceless: Faith-based Organizations Tackle Human Rights Issues
Source/Citation: KAICIID. “Voice of the Voiceless: Faith-based Organizations Tackle Human Rights Issues.” International Dialogue Centre (KAICIID), 10 December 2020.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: Faith-based organisations can play an important role in promoting human rights through their connections with local communities. This feature discusses how religious groups address discrimination, religious freedom and hate speech, while identifying challenges such as limited cooperation and legal expertise. It highlights the importance of dialogue across different faiths, human rights education, and translating religious concerns into language that can support wider public advocacy.

Title: International Law and the Global South
Source/Citation: The Looking Glass. “International Law and the Global South.” Featuring Obiora Chinedu Okafor. Produced by Kosi Ogbuli. Podcast episode, 13 February 2023, 44 minutes.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: This episode discusses how international law has been shaped by European colonialism and unequal global power relations. Professor Obiora Chinedu Okafor considers the criticism that international legal institutions have contributed to injustice and exploitation, and the importance of examining international law from Global South perspectives. The conversation raises questions about how international law might better address inequality and recognise perspectives historically marginalised in its development.

Title: Can the Global South Salvage International Law?
Source/Citation: McMahon, Kate. “Can the Global South Salvage International Law?” The New Humanitarian, 9 December 2025.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: The article examines how Global South countries are responding to concerns about the unequal enforcement of international law, particularly in relation to Palestine. McMahon focuses on the Hague Group, comparing its efforts with earlier movements for cooperation among formerly colonised countries. She discusses the political and economic obstacles these countries face and questions whether collective action can make international legal institutions more accountable and effective.

Title: Tailoring the Message: How the Political Left and Right Think Differently About Human Rights
Source/Citation: Braun, Joe, and Stephen Arves. “Tailoring the Message: How the Political Left and Right Think Differently About Human Rights.” OpenGlobalRights, 10 August 2017.
Theme: Grassroots Movements & Participation; Democracy & Political Power; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Braun and Arves examine how political views influence people's responses to human rights messages. Based on experiments with US participants, they found that personal accounts of suffering were more effective among liberal respondents, while graphic images of abuse had a greater impact on conservative respondents. Their findings suggest that human rights organisations need to consider their audiences when communicating about rights violations and encouraging public support.

Title: Faith-Based Cooperation Is Vital to Uphold Human Rights for All
Source/Citation: Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR). “Faith-Based Cooperation Is Vital to Uphold Human Rights for All.” 3 February 2025.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: Religious communities can work together to promote human rights, reduce discrimination and strengthen trust across different beliefs. This OHCHR article introduces the UN's Faith for Rights initiative, which encourages religious leaders and organisations to learn from one another and take practical action. It describes examples of interfaith cooperation, including work in Cyprus, and highlights educational tools for addressing religious intolerance and hate speech.

Title: Faith for Rights Framework
Source/Citation: OHCHR. Faith for Rights Framework. 2017–ongoing.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Human Rights Futures & Theory; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: The Faith for Rights framework brings together religious leaders, faith-based organisations and human rights actors to promote equality and respect across different beliefs. It encourages cooperation between communities and connects religious teachings with international human rights principles. The initiative provides a shared approach for addressing discrimination, supporting religious freedom and promoting human rights through dialogue and collective action.

Title: The Power of Religion and Human Rights: Larry Cox at the Bernstein Symposium at Yale University
Source/Citation: Cox, Larry. “The Power of Religion and Human Rights: Larry Cox at the Bernstein Symposium at Yale University.” Kairos Center, 6 July 2017. Originally delivered as a keynote address on 23 March 2017.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Larry Cox examines the relationship between religion, human rights and social movements. He argues that the growing emphasis on legal expertise and professional advocacy has weakened parts of the human rights movement's connection to grassroots struggles. Drawing on civil rights activism and campaigns against poverty, he discusses how religious and secular groups can work together to address inequality, strengthen community leadership and pursue broader social change.

Title: Sources of Basic Human Rights Ideas: A Christian Perspective
Source/Citation: Stackhouse, Max L. “Sources of Basic Human Rights Ideas: A Christian Perspective.” Lecture transcript, Pew Research Center, 27 January 2003.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Human Rights Futures & Theory; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Stackhouse examines the historical and theological connections between Christianity and modern human rights. He argues that Christian ideas about human dignity, moral responsibility and individual freedom have contributed to the development of universal rights. He also discusses how religious traditions and human rights principles can support pluralism, while questioning whether human rights can maintain their authority without a deeper moral or religious foundation.

Title: Faith-based Organisations Are Key Advocates for Human Rights
Source/Citation: Schwabe, Frank. “Faith-based Organisations Are Key Advocates for Human Rights.” Speech delivered at PaRD's Annual Forum on Religion and Sustainable Development 2023, published by the International Partnership on Religion and Sustainable Development, 2 November 2023.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Climate & Environmental Justice
Key Takeaway: Faith-based organisations can contribute to human rights protection through community advocacy, humanitarian assistance and cooperation with governments and civil society. In this speech, Frank Schwabe highlights their work on poverty, religious freedom and environmental justice, including a case involving Indigenous communities affected by mining in Guatemala. He also discusses the importance of protecting religious human rights defenders and involving faith communities in international development partnerships.

Title: Religion and Rights: Inside the Movements Reclaiming Gender Justice
Source/Citation: Petersen, Marie Juul, and Kaja Borchgrevink. “Religion and Rights: Inside the Movements Reclaiming Gender Justice.” OpenGlobalRights, 8 May 2026.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Gender & Social Justice; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: Religious beliefs and gender equality are not necessarily in conflict. Petersen and Borchgrevink examine how feminist theologians, LGBTQ+ activists and faith-based organisations challenge discriminatory religious interpretations and promote gender justice. Through examples from Africa, Asia and Latin America, they describe how activists reinterpret religious teachings, create more inclusive communities and connect human rights advocacy with religious traditions, often while facing opposition from both religious conservatives and secular movements.

Title: Peace and Justice: Human Rights in Catholic Thought
Source/Citation: Urmston, Benjamin J. “Peace and Justice: Human Rights in Catholic Thought.” Xavier University, April 2014.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Economic & Development Justice
Key Takeaway: Urmston explores how Catholic social teaching connects human dignity with economic justice, peace and human rights. He argues that civil and political freedoms cannot be fully enjoyed without access to basic necessities such as food, housing, healthcare and employment. The resource also discusses solidarity, environmental responsibility and the importance of cooperation between governments, religious communities and citizens in building a more just international order.

Title: Palestine and the Limits of International Law
Source/Citation: Krever, Tor. “Palestine and the Limits of International Law.” Revista Crítica de Ciências Sociais, no. 137 (2025): 193–210.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Accountability & Reparations
Key Takeaway: Krever examines the limitations of international law in addressing violence and injustice in Palestine. He argues that focusing on the prosecution of individual political leaders can overlook the broader structures that enable violence. The article also considers proposals for a Gaza Tribunal and the history of people's tribunals, questioning whether legal approaches to accountability can support broader political struggles or risk narrowing their aims.

Title: Could This Truly Be the End of Universalism? Starting 2026 with Reflections on Gaza, the Maduro Abduction, and Some of the World’s Neglected Conflicts (Sudan, Tigray, Yemen, Myanmar, and the Uyghurs)
Source/Citation: Risse, Mathias. “Could This Truly Be the End of Universalism? Starting 2026 with Reflections on Gaza, the Maduro Abduction, and Some of the World’s Neglected Conflicts (Sudan, Tigray, Yemen, Myanmar, and the Uyghurs).” Carr-Ryan Center for Human Rights, Harvard Kennedy School, 11 January 2026.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Global Governance & International Law; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: Risse examines the growing challenges to universal human rights principles through conflicts in Gaza, Venezuela and other regions receiving limited international attention. He argues that selective enforcement, unequal political power and inconsistent responses to human suffering are weakening confidence in international law. Rather than abandoning universalism, he calls for its renewal through more consistent legal standards, institutional reform and greater recognition of global inequalities.

Title: Third World Approaches to International Law Review (TWAILR)
Source/Citation: TWAILR Editorial Collective. Third World Approaches to International Law Review (TWAILR). Independent open-access journal and publishing platform, established 2019.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: The Third World Approaches to International Law Review (TWAILR) provides an open-access platform for scholarship examining international law from Global South perspectives. It publishes research and commentary on colonialism, inequality, resistance and alternative approaches to global governance. By prioritising perspectives often marginalised in legal scholarship, TWAILR seeks to make international legal debates more inclusive and support the development of more equitable legal frameworks.

Title: States and Self-Determination
Source/Citation: Shahabuddin, Mohammad. “States and Self-Determination.” In Research Handbook on Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL), edited by Antony Anghie, B. S. Chimni, Michael Fakhri, Karin Mickelson and Vasuki Nesiah, 277–288. Edward Elgar Publishing, 2025.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Indigenous Rights & Knowledge
Key Takeaway: Shahabuddin challenges the assumption that European models of statehood can be applied universally. Using Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL), he examines how colonial boundaries and political ideas influenced the formation of postcolonial states. The chapter argues that these processes have restricted self-determination for minority communities and highlights the importance of examining inequalities within postcolonial states, not only between states.

Title: Research Handbook on Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL)
Source/Citation: Anghie, Antony, B. S. Chimni, Michael Fakhri, Karin Mickelson, and Vasuki Nesiah, eds. Research Handbook on Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL). Research Handbooks in International Law. Edward Elgar Publishing, 2025.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: This handbook brings together scholarship on Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL), examining how colonial histories and global inequalities continue to shape international legal rules and institutions. Its chapters address human rights, development, economic relations, climate change and other areas of international law. The collection explores how perspectives from the Global South can challenge established legal assumptions and contribute to alternative approaches to international law and global justice.

Title: Disruption and Emergence: How to Think About Human Rights Futures
Source/Citation: Choi-Fitzpatrick, Austin. “Disruption and Emergence: How to Think About Human Rights Futures.” Journal of Human Rights 23, no. 1 (2024): 105–123.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Climate & Environmental Justice; Digital Rights & Technology
Key Takeaway: Choi-Fitzpatrick examines how changes in geopolitics, climate, energy, science and technology could transform the future of human rights. He suggests that these developments may mark the beginning of a new era, rather than simply another stage in the evolution of existing rights. The article explores ways to understand such transformations and proposes hypotheses and practical recommendations for anticipating possible changes.

Title: “Faith for Rights”: A Framework for Rights-Based Sustainable Engagement with Faith Actors
Source/Citation: Salama, Ibrahim, and Michael Wiener. “‘Faith for Rights’: A Framework for Rights-Based Sustainable Engagement with Faith Actors.” Religion & Development 3, no. 2 (2024): 221–235. Published online 16 June 2025.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Salama and Wiener examine how the Faith for Rights framework connects religious communities with international human rights principles. They discuss the Beirut Declaration, its 18 commitments and the #Faith4Rights toolkit, which encourages practical cooperation and learning among participants. The article describes how these resources have been used by different institutions and proposes strengthening networks for continued dialogue, knowledge-sharing and joint action.

Title: ‘Faith for Rights’ in Armed Conflict: Lessons from Practice
Source/Citation: Salama, Ibrahim, and Michael Wiener. “‘Faith for Rights’ in Armed Conflict: Lessons from Practice.” Journal of Human Rights Practice 17, no. 2 (July 2025), article huad015. First published online 7 June 2023.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Gender & Social Justice
Key Takeaway: Salama and Wiener examine how the Faith for Rights framework has been applied in situations of armed conflict. Through examples from Afghanistan, Cyprus and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, they discuss the role of religious actors in addressing human rights challenges and promoting dialogue. The article also explores how practical exercises and shared learning can support conflict mediation, cooperation and the prevention of incitement to hatred.

Title: Human Rights and Faith: A ‘World-Wide Secular Religion’?
Source/Citation: Féron, Henri. “Human Rights and Faith: A ‘World-Wide Secular Religion’?” Ethics & Global Politics 7, no. 4 (2014): 181–200.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Féron examines the similarities between human rights and religious belief, arguing that both depend on moral convictions that cannot be conclusively proven. He discusses how this creates tensions between human rights and other cultural or religious values. The article warns that imposing human rights through coercion can undermine their own principles and emphasises the importance of tolerance and mutual respect.

Title: Identity and Dignity Within the Human Rights Discourse: An Anthropological and Praxis Approach
Source/Citation: Louw, D.J., 2014, ‘Identity and dignity within the human rights discourse: An anthropological and praxis approach’, Verbum et Ecclesia 35(2), Art. #876, 9 pages.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Louw examines human dignity as something more fundamental than legal rights, connecting it to people's search for meaning, identity and relationships with others. Drawing on Christian theology, he proposes an understanding of dignity that moves beyond conventional moral and legal frameworks to consider how human worth is experienced and expressed in everyday life.

Title: International Law and Its Discontents: Rethinking the Global South
Source/Citation: Rajagopal, Balakrishnan. “International Law and Its Discontents: Rethinking the Global South.” Proceedings of the ASIL Annual Meeting 106 (2012): 176–181.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: Rajagopal examines how international law has contributed to global inequalities and distinguishes between powerful Global South states and grassroots movements challenging existing structures. He argues that the growing influence of emerging economies does not necessarily lead to a fairer international order. The essay also questions prevailing models of economic development and considers how social movements could contribute to more democratic international governance.

Title: International Law as a Discipline in Crisis
Source/Citation: Tzouvala, Ntina. “International Law as a Discipline in Crisis.” Australian Journal of International Affairs 79, no. 1 (2025): 71–78.
Theme: Global Governance & International Law; Human Rights Futures & Theory; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Tzouvala revisits longstanding criticism of international law's tendency to focus on major crises. Examining scholarly responses to the war in Gaza, she argues that disagreements now extend beyond how international law should respond to violence to whether particular events are recognised as crises at all. The article explores how these divisions challenge shared assumptions within the discipline.

Title: Liberation Theology: Practice of a People Hungering for Human Dignity
Source/Citation: Pineda, Ana Maria. “Liberation Theology: Practice of a People Hungering for Human Dignity.” The Way 38, no. 3 (1998): 231–239.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Pineda examines liberation theology as a form of Christian practice rooted in struggles against poverty, oppression and marginalisation. She explains how experiences of injustice and actions taken to challenge it shape theological reflection, rather than the other way around. Although historically associated with Latin America, liberation theology is presented as an approach that can emerge wherever communities seek liberation from oppression.

Title: Re-enchanting International Law is a Global South Project
Source/Citation: O’Malley, Alanna. “Re-enchanting International Law Is a Global South Project.” Opinio Juris, 6 December 2025.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: O’Malley examines how Global South countries have used international legal institutions to challenge colonialism and unequal power relations. Drawing on historical efforts to end South African control over Namibia and more recent cases concerning Palestine and climate change, she argues that these initiatives demonstrate international law's potential for transformation. The article presents Global South leadership as central to developing a more inclusive and accountable international order.

Title: The Right to a Healthy Environment and the Global South
Source/Citation: Gonzalez, Carmen G. “The Right to a Healthy Environment and the Global South.” AJIL Unbound 117 (2023): 173–178.
Theme: Climate & Environmental Justice; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Indigenous Rights & Knowledge
Key Takeaway: Gonzalez examines the Global South's role in developing the right to a healthy environment and how regional human rights courts have interpreted it. She considers whether these legal developments can address limitations of traditional human rights approaches, including their emphasis on individuals over communities, their human-centred understanding of nature, and their difficulties in responding to environmental harm across borders and economic structures.
