Title: UN Recognition of the Human Right to a Healthy Environment
Source/Citation: AJIL Unbound. “Symposium on UN Recognition of the Human Right to a Healthy Environment.” Vol. 117 (2023): 162–198. Cambridge University Press.
Theme: Climate & Environmental Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: This symposium examines the implications of UN recognition of the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. Its contributors consider how the right may influence international and regional law, environmental accountability and the development of new legal standards. The essays also explore its limitations, particularly in relation to economic inequality, environmental destruction, the rights of nature and the protection of future generations.

Title: Disruptive Behavior in the Postdisciplinary Society
Source/Citation: Gaete-Silva, Joaquin, and Alfredo Gaete. “Disruptive Behavior in the Postdisciplinary Society.” Frontiers in Psychology 12 (2021): Article 740856.
Theme: Education & Knowledge Justice; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: Gaete-Silva and Gaete examine changing attitudes towards disruptive behaviour, punishment and authority in contemporary societies. They argue that traditional disciplinary responses have lost social legitimacy and may worsen the problems they seek to address. The article connects these changes to evolving understandings of justice, individual rights and social participation, and considers alternative ways of responding to disruptive behaviour.

Title: Evaluating the Value of TWAIL, Environmental Justice, and Decolonization Discourses as Framing Lenses for International Environmental Law
Source/Citation: Humby, Tracy-Lynn. “Evaluating the Value of TWAIL, Environmental Justice, and Decolonization Discourses as Framing Lenses for International Environmental Law.” Transnational Law & Contemporary Problems 26, no. 2 (2017): 317–342.
Theme: Climate & Environmental Justice; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Humby examines TWAIL, environmental justice and decolonisation as distinct but overlapping approaches to international environmental law. Drawing on South Africa's 2015–2016 student movement and debates surrounding Africa's renewable energy transition, she explores how these frameworks can illuminate different dimensions of inequality and power. The article applies them to issues including oil and gas concessions and renewable energy trade disputes.

Title: Human Rights and the Nation State in the Global South: A Genealogical and Decolonial Critique
Source/Citation: Woldeyes, Yirga Gelaw. “Human Rights and the Nation State in the Global South: A Genealogical and Decolonial Critique.” Journal of Human Rights 24, no. 5 (2025): 499–511.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Democracy & Political Power; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Woldeyes examines how international human rights law relies on nation-states for the recognition and protection of rights, despite the colonial origins of state institutions across much of the Global South. Drawing on African experiences, he argues that this arrangement can obscure violence carried out by states themselves. The article proposes rethinking human rights beyond state-centred frameworks to make them more meaningful for marginalised communities.

Title: Addressing Colonial Crimes in the Third World: The Imperatives and Potentials of a TWAIL Paradigm
Source/Citation: Iyi, John-Mark, and Linda Mushoriwa. “Addressing Colonial Crimes in the Third World: The Imperatives and Potentials of a TWAIL Paradigm.” In International Criminal Law and the Legacy of Colonialism: An African Perspective, edited by Pilisano Harris Masake and Florian Jeßberger, 5–28. Berlin: Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, 2024.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Iyi and Mushoriwa examine whether contemporary international law can adequately address atrocities committed during colonial rule. They focus particularly on the intertemporal rule, which complicates legal accountability for historical crimes. Drawing on TWAIL, they explore alternative approaches to international criminal justice that take demands for accountability and redress from formerly colonised communities more seriously.

Title: International Criminal Law and the Legacy of Colonialism: An African Perspective
Source/Citation: Masake, Pilisano, and Florian Jeßberger, eds. International Criminal Law and the Legacy of Colonialism: An African Perspective. In cooperation with Luca Hauffe. Berlin: Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, 2024.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Accountability & Reparations; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: This edited volume brings together predominantly African scholars to examine the relationship between international criminal justice and colonialism. It considers whether contemporary institutions reproduce colonial power relations, how African approaches to accountability might inform alternative models of justice, and whether international criminal law can address historical colonial crimes. The contributions also explore the roles of African judges and perspectives in shaping international criminal justice.

Title: Liberation Theology and Liberal Society
Source/Citation: Goulet, Denis. “Liberation Theology and Liberal Society.” Notre Dame Journal of Law, Ethics & Public Policy 2, no. 1 (1987): 43–53.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Economic & Development Justice
Key Takeaway: Goulet examines liberation theology as a response to economic exploitation, political oppression and structural injustice in Latin America. He traces its development through religious thought and grassroots struggles, highlighting how collective action informs theological reflection. The essay also critiques inequalities associated with liberal capitalism and presents liberation theology as a means of connecting Christian faith with social transformation and the defence of human rights.

Title: The Occupation of Palestine from a TWAIL Lens
Source/Citation: Murphy, Ray, Anita Ferrara, and Susan Power. “The Occupation of Palestine from a TWAIL Lens.” In Prolonged Occupation and International Law: Israel and Palestine, chapter 3. Brill, 2023.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Accountability & Reparations
Key Takeaway: Murphy, Ferrara and Power apply TWAIL to examine how international law operates in the context of Israel's prolonged occupation of Palestine. They critique the use of legal arguments to justify military practices and examine how Israeli judicial decisions may reinforce interpretations that favour military authority. The chapter considers how international legal institutions and scholarship can contribute to maintaining unequal power relations.

Title: Scholars, States, and Human Rights: A Comparison of Third World Approaches to International Law with Diverging State-Actors’ Stances in the UN Human Rights Council
Source/Citation: Weingand, Yanik. “Scholars, States, and Human Rights: A Comparison of Third World Approaches to International Law with Diverging State-Actors’ Stances in the UN Human Rights Council.” Global Europe – Basel Papers on Europe in a Global Perspective, no. 122 (2022).
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: Weingand compares criticisms of the international human rights system advanced by TWAIL scholars with those expressed by China, Cuba and Egypt during the first three cycles of the UN Universal Periodic Review. He organises TWAIL scholarship around critiques of culture, rhetoric and institutional models, then uses qualitative content analysis to investigate similarities between academic and state-level arguments.

Title: The Plurality of Truth in Post-Conflict Societies and the ‘Right to Truth’ in International Law
Source/Citation: Wijenayake, Vishakha. “The Plurality of Truth in Post-Conflict Societies and the ‘Right to Truth’ in International Law.” Sri Lanka Journal of International Law 26 (2018): 31–52.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Wijenayake examines how understandings of truth differ within post-conflict societies and how these differences affect transitional justice. Tracing the right to truth through international humanitarian and human rights law, she argues that legal approaches should recognise multiple dimensions of truth rather than assume a single, uniform understanding. The article explores how the right might respond to the particular needs of different post-conflict contexts.

Title: TWAIL, Archives, and Refugee Law
Source/Citation: Ramasubramanyam, Jay. “TWAIL, Archives, and Refugee Law.” Journal of Refugee Studies 37, no. 4 (2024): 994–1007.
Theme: Migration & Displacement; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Ramasubramanyam combines TWAIL and archival research to challenge Eurocentric accounts of international refugee law. Focusing on India's refugee-hosting practices and its resistance to dominant international legal frameworks, he explores alternative histories and understandings of refugee protection. The article presents archival research as a means of recovering perspectives marginalised in conventional legal histories and reconsidering how international refugee law is studied.

Title: “Let Us All Agree to Die a Little”: TWAIL’s Unfulfilled Promise
Source/Citation: Modirzadeh, Naz Khatoon. “‘Let Us All Agree to Die a Little’: TWAIL’s Unfulfilled Promise.” Harvard International Law Journal 65, no. 1 (Winter 2023): 79–131.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Modirzadeh examines the gap between TWAIL's ambition to transform international law and its practical influence on Global South political agency. While acknowledging its contributions to exposing colonial structures, she argues that TWAIL has struggled to develop coherent strategies for change. She identifies unresolved questions concerning state power, political violence and representation, and proposes alternative directions for translating critical scholarship into collective action.

Title: Breaking the Echo Chambers of Transitional Justice and TWAIL: An Intellectual and Policy Exchange
Source/Citation: Aboueldahab, Noha. “Breaking the Echo Chambers of Transitional Justice and TWAIL: An Intellectual and Policy Exchange.” International Journal of Transitional Justice 19, no. 1 (2025): 135–150.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Aboueldahab examines the limitations of transitional justice and TWAIL, arguing that both fields have become constrained by insular debates and unrepresentative knowledge production. She proposes greater exchange between TWAIL's critical approaches to international law and transitional justice's practical orientation towards institutional and policy change. The article explores how this dialogue could help develop more inclusive understandings of justice and resistance.

Title: Finding a Place for TWAIL in African Studies
Source/Citation: Bunting, Annie, and Cajetan Iheka. “Finding a Place for TWAIL in African Studies.” African Studies Review 67, no. 3 (2024): 535–540.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Bunting and Iheka encourage greater engagement between TWAIL and African Studies, highlighting their shared interests in colonial histories, self-determination, economic exploitation and African agency. They argue that closer interdisciplinary exchange could enrich understandings of international law and its effects on African societies, while creating more space for critical legal scholarship within African Studies.

Title: Human Security, TWAIL, and the Importance of Self-Reflection in Our Own Scholarship
Source/Citation: Gilder, Alexander. “Human Security, TWAIL, and the Importance of Self-Reflection in Our Own Scholarship.” New York University Journal of International Law and Politics 54, no. 1 (2021): 1–13.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Gilder revisits his earlier work on human security through TWAIL scholarship, examining whether people-centred approaches can reproduce the colonial assumptions of international law. He argues that human security should prioritise communities' own understandings of their needs and enable their participation in decisions affecting them. The article also emphasises scholarly self-reflection as a way to challenge dominant assumptions in international legal research and teaching.

Title: Liberation Theology: Religion, Reform, and Revolution
Source/Citation: Central Intelligence Agency, Directorate of Intelligence. Liberation Theology: Religion, Reform, and Revolution: A Research Paper. GI 86-10028. Washington, DC: CIA, April 1986.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: This CIA research paper examines liberation theology as a force for political and social change, particularly in Latin America. It considers how Christian grassroots organising, demands for socioeconomic reform and relationships with revolutionary movements could influence existing political structures. Written from a US intelligence perspective, the report reveals how liberation theology's mobilisation of marginalised communities was interpreted within Cold War security debates.

Title: Narrative Injustice and the Legal Erasure of Indigeneity: A TWAIL Reframing of the Kashmiri Pandit Case in Postcolonial International Law
Source/Citation: Pandey, Shilpi. “Narrative Injustice and the Legal Erasure of Indigeneity: A TWAIL Reframing of the Kashmiri Pandit Case in Postcolonial International Law.” Laws 14 (2025): Article 96.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice
Key Takeaway: Pandey examines the legal recognition of Kashmiri Pandits through TWAIL, focusing on Indigenous rights and internal displacement. She argues that state narratives and geopolitical considerations have contributed to the community's exclusion from international protection frameworks. Drawing on legal analysis and displacement-related evidence, the article calls for greater attention to epistemic justice and the role of narratives in determining whose experiences receive legal recognition.

Title: After Truth, After Shame… After Information Politics? Rethinking the Epistemologies of Human Rights in the Digital-Authoritarian Conjuncture
Source/Citation: Bowsher, Josh. “After Truth, After Shame… After Information Politics? Rethinking the Epistemologies of Human Rights in the Digital-Authoritarian Conjuncture.” The International Journal of Human Rights 28, nos. 8–9 (2024): 1501–1525.
Theme: Digital Rights & Technology; Education & Knowledge Justice; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Bowsher examines how post-truth politics and reactionary digital cultures challenge human rights advocacy strategies based on documenting abuses and publicly shaming governments. Drawing on Donna Haraway and Maurizio Lazzarato, he proposes a more situated and politically engaged approach to producing human rights knowledge. The article considers how advocacy might move beyond reliance on factual exposure alone.

Title: Introduction: Transitional Justice and Corporate Accountability
Source/Citation: Payne, Leigh A., Gabriel Pereira, and Laura Bernal-Bermúdez. “Introduction: Transitional Justice and Corporate Accountability.” In Transitional Justice and Corporate Accountability from Below: Deploying Archimedes’ Lever, 1–20. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2020.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Economic & Development Justice; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: Payne, Pereira and Bernal-Bermúdez introduce a model of corporate accountability that emphasises the role of civil society and institutional actors in pursuing justice for corporate involvement in human rights violations. They examine obstacles to accountability, including business resistance and limited international pressure, and explain how grassroots demands and institutional innovation can create opportunities for accountability through courts and truth commissions.

Title: Beyond Symbolic Recognition: Readdressing Germany’s Long Way Ahead in Taking Responsibility for the Genocide in Namibia
Source/Citation: Girardini, Sophie, Veronika Stockinger, and Franziska Michel. “Beyond Symbolic Recognition: Readdressing Germany’s Long Way Ahead in Taking Responsibility for the Genocide in Namibia.” Völkerrechtsblog, 28 May 2026.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Indigenous Rights & Knowledge
Key Takeaway: Girardini, Stockinger and Michel examine Germany's response to the colonial genocide in Namibia, focusing on reparations, remembrance and education. They challenge Germany's reliance on historical legal standards to dispute compensation obligations and highlight the exclusion of affected communities from negotiations. The authors argue that meaningful transitional justice requires more than symbolic recognition, including reparations, public education and community participation.

Title: International Rulings and the UK–Mauritius Chagos Agreement: The Road to the 2025 UK–Mauritius Agreement
Source/Citation: Afogo, Nouwagnon Olivier. “International Rulings and the UK–Mauritius Chagos Agreement: The Road to the 2025 UK–Mauritius Agreement.” Verfassungsblog, 27 July 2025.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Accountability & Reparations; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Afogo examines how international judicial decisions contributed to the 2025 UK–Mauritius agreement concerning the Chagos Archipelago. Drawing on rulings from the ICJ, maritime arbitration and ITLOS, he explores their influence on the recognition of Mauritian sovereignty and the right to self-determination. The blog post also considers the agreement's provisions on reparations and the possibilities for Chagossian resettlement.

Title: Reparations
Source/Citation: Ferstman, Carla. “Reparations.” Oxford Bibliographies in International Law. Oxford University Press, 23 March 2012.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Ferstman outlines the legal principles and purposes of reparations for internationally wrongful acts. She explains different forms of redress, including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation and satisfaction, alongside guarantees of non-repetition. The article highlights how reparations can address past harm, restore dignity and relationships, and contribute to preventing future violations through institutional and legal reform.

Title: When Decolonization Meets Human Rights: CERD’s 2025 Decision on the Chagos Agreement
Source/Citation: Tranchez, Elodie. “When Decolonization Meets Human Rights: CERD’s 2025 Decision on the Chagos Agreement.” EJIL:Talk!, 18 December 2025.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Accountability & Reparations; Indigenous Rights & Knowledge
Key Takeaway: Tranchez examines the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination's intervention concerning the 2025 UK–Mauritius Chagos Agreement. She highlights concerns about the exclusion of Chagossian communities from negotiations and restrictions on their return to Diego Garcia. The blog post considers how decolonisation agreements must address the rights and participation of displaced communities, rather than territorial sovereignty alone.

Title: Teaching International Law When the Ground Is Moving
Source/Citation: Fofana, Idriss. “Teaching International Law When the Ground Is Moving.” EJIL:Talk!, 1 December 2025.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Education & Knowledge Justice; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Fofana questions approaches to teaching international law that focus on exceptional crises or defending established legal rules. He presents international law as continually shaped by political struggles, competing interpretations and historical change. Drawing on the evolution of self-determination, he argues for greater attention to how legal principles are developed, contested and used for different political purposes.

Title: Dialogue as Governance: The First UN Dialogue on Global AI Governance and Its Implications for Human Rights
Source/Citation: Ayalew, Yohannes Eneyew, José-Miguel Bello y Villarino, and Fleur Johns. “Dialogue as Governance: The First UN Dialogue on Global AI Governance and Its Implications for Human Rights.” EJIL:Talk!, 16 October 2026.
Theme: Digital Rights & Technology; Global Governance & International Law; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: Ayalew, Bello y Villarino and Johns examine the first UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance and its potential to support more inclusive international cooperation. They highlight disagreements over human rights protections, unequal access to AI technologies and the influence of powerful states and corporations. The authors question whether the Dialogue can move beyond discussion to strengthen accountability and participation, particularly for developing countries and marginalised communities.

Title: Apportioning Historical Responsibility After the ICJ’s Climate Advisory Opinion: From Principle to Practice
Source/Citation: Halder, Tonmoy. “Apportioning Historical Responsibility After the ICJ’s Climate Advisory Opinion: From Principle to Practice.” EJIL:Talk!, 24 August 2026.
Theme: Climate & Environmental Justice; Accountability & Reparations; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Halder examines how responsibility for climate-related harm could be allocated among states following the ICJ's 2025 Climate Advisory Opinion. Drawing on principles of state responsibility, earlier judicial opinions and climate attribution science, he proposes a two-stage approach to assessing collective contributions and individual liability. The article considers the challenges of translating historical emissions into legally justified claims for reparations.

Title: Institutional Discretion, Due Process and the Common Heritage of Humankind: The First Provisional Measures Orders in NORI and TOML v. the Authority
Source/Citation: Salamanca-Aguado, M. E. “Institutional Discretion, Due Process, and the Common Heritage of Humankind: The First Provisional Measures Orders in NORI and TOML v. the Authority.” EJIL:Talk!, 2026.
Theme: Global Governance & International Law; Climate & Environmental Justice; Accountability & Reparations
Key Takeaway: Salamanca-Aguado examines the first provisional measures orders concerning the International Seabed Authority's supervision of deep-sea mining contractors. The article explains how the Seabed Disputes Chamber balanced the Authority's regulatory powers with contractors' procedural rights, while interpreting both within the common heritage of humankind framework. It highlights the importance of institutional accountability and procedural fairness in governing seabed resources.

Title: Disaster Displacement and International Protection in the EU: Challenges, Misconceptions, and the Way Forward
Source/Citation: Scissa, Chiara. Disaster Displacement and International Protection in the EU: Challenges, Misconceptions, and the Way Forward. London: Routledge, 2026.
Theme: Migration & Displacement; Climate & Environmental Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Scissa examines why EU asylum systems struggle to protect people displaced across borders by disasters. Drawing on legislation, policies and case law, particularly from Italy, she identifies problems in how disaster-related harm is understood, how protection criteria are applied and how restrictive asylum policies limit access to protection. The book advocates more flexible interpretations of existing legal frameworks.

Title: Chagos Archipelago Residents Deserve Reparations, Not Regrets
Source/Citation: Ngari, Allan, and Clive Baldwin. “Chagos Archipelago Residents Deserve Reparations, Not Regrets.” Human Rights Watch, 28 August 2025. Originally published in Mail & Guardian.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Indigenous Rights & Knowledge
Key Takeaway: Ngari and Baldwin critique the 2025 UK–Mauritius Chagos Agreement for prioritising territorial sovereignty while leaving key Chagossian rights unresolved. They highlight restrictions on return, inadequate guarantees of compensation and limited community participation in future governance. The authors argue that addressing colonial displacement requires meaningful reparations and the involvement of affected communities, rather than symbolic recognition alone.

Title: A Post-Humanist and Anti-Capitalist Understanding of the Rights of Nature (with a Coda about the Commons)
Source/Citation: Lloredo Alix, Luis. “A Post-Humanist and Anti-Capitalist Understanding of the Rights of Nature (with a Coda about the Commons).” Oñati Socio-Legal Series 13, no. 3 (2023): 1003–1035.
Theme: Climate & Environmental Justice; Economic & Development Justice; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Lloredo Alix argues that recognising the rights of nature requires rethinking conventional legal understandings of rights. Drawing on post-humanist, anti-capitalist and postcolonial perspectives, he challenges approaches centred on human interests, individual ownership and European legal traditions. The article presents natural entities as potential rights-holders and considers how ecological understandings of rights may transform legal relationships between humans and the natural world.

Title: 70 Years of Decoloniality: Epistemic Disobedience and Global Public Health
Source/Citation: McGovern, Justine, and Lisa Fusco. “70 Years of Decoloniality: Epistemic Disobedience and Global Public Health.” Frontiers in Public Health 13 (2025), article 1658591.
Theme: Education & Knowledge Justice; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Economic & Development Justice
Key Takeaway: McGovern and Fusco examine how epistemic disobedience, a concept developed by Walter Mignolo, can inform decolonial approaches to public health research and practice. They challenge colonial hierarchies in knowledge production and consider alternative approaches to research that recognise different experiences and perspectives. The article connects these debates to efforts to advance health equity as a human right.

Title: Epistemologies of the South and Human Rights: Santos and the Quest for Global and Cognitive Justice
Source/Citation: Barreto, José-Manuel. “Epistemologies of the South and Human Rights: Santos and the Quest for Global and Cognitive Justice.” Indiana Journal of Global Legal Studies 21, no. 2 (2014): 395–422.
Theme: Education & Knowledge Justice; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Barreto examines Boaventura de Sousa Santos's ideas of abyssal thinking and Epistemologies of the South to reconsider the foundations of human rights. He challenges the exclusion of non-Western knowledge and experiences from dominant rights frameworks, exploring how colonial histories and intercultural dialogue can inform a more inclusive, post-abyssal understanding of human rights.

Title: The Prospect of an International Binding Treaty on the Right to Development: A Gateway to Global Justice
Source/Citation: Tadeg, Mesenbet Assefa. “The Prospect of an International Binding Treaty on the Right to Development: A Gateway to Global Justice.” African Human Rights Law Journal 25, no. 2 (2025): 485–512.
Theme: Economic & Development Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Tadeg examines the proposed International Covenant on the Right to Development as a framework for addressing global inequalities. He argues that discussions should move beyond recognising the right towards its practical implementation, particularly in relation to international trade, intellectual property, debt, climate finance and development financing. The article considers how binding international commitments could strengthen the realisation of the right to development.

Title: Against Temporal Abstractions: The Battle for Colonial and Climate Reparations in International Law
Source/Citation: Cusato, Eliana. “Against Temporal Abstractions: The Battle for Colonial and Climate Reparations in International Law.” International Journal of Law in Context 21, no. 2 (2025): 281–299.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Climate & Environmental Justice; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Cusato examines how international law's understanding of time shapes claims for colonial and climate reparations. She argues that legal concepts of responsibility, causation and remedies reflect linear and abstract notions of time that can obscure connections between historical injustices and continuing harm. The article explores how reparations claims challenge these assumptions by linking unequal pasts, presents and futures.

Title: Ending the Past: International Law, Intertemporality, and Reparations for Past Wrongs
Source/Citation: Fuhrmann, Rémi, and Melissa Schweizer. “Ending the Past: International Law, Intertemporality, and Reparations for Past Wrongs.” German Law Journal 26, no. 8 (2025): 1539–1559.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Fuhrmann and Schweizer challenge the assumption that intertemporal law necessarily prevents reparations for historical injustices. Drawing on international judicial decisions, state practice and legal scholarship, they identify more dynamic interpretations of the doctrine that recognise the relationship between past wrongs and continuing harm. The article considers how these interpretations could support claims for reparations relating to colonialism and slavery.

Title: Law, Time, and (In)justice After Empire: Germany’s Objection to Colonial Reparations and the Chronopolitics of Deflection
Source/Citation: Graf, Sinja. “Law, Time, and (In)justice After Empire: Germany’s Objection to Colonial Reparations and the Chronopolitics of Deflection.” International Theory 17, no. 1 (2025): 1–28.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Graf examines how Germany has invoked international law's rules on non-retroactivity to resist reparations claims arising from its colonial genocide in Namibia. Drawing on parliamentary records, she develops the concept of chronopolitics of deflection to show how legal arguments about time can redirect demands for reparations towards development assistance, limiting recognition of historical responsibility and continuing injustice.

Title: States Before Their Colonial Past: Practice in Addressing Responsibility
Source/Citation: Marconi, Rachele. “States Before Their Colonial Past: Practice in Addressing Responsibility.” Questions of International Law (QIL), Zoom-out 103 (2024): 25–46.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Marconi examines how former colonial powers have responded to demands for accountability for historical injustices. She identifies a tendency to acknowledge moral or historical responsibility through apologies, symbolic measures and negotiated arrangements while avoiding recognition of legal obligations. The article considers whether these evolving but inconsistent state practices could contribute to future international standards on colonial reparations.

Title: Beyond Redemption? Problematising the Critique of Human Rights in Contemporary International Legal Thought
Source/Citation: Golder, Ben. “Beyond Redemption? Problematising the Critique of Human Rights in Contemporary International Legal Thought.” London Review of International Law 2, no. 1 (2014): 77–114.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Golder examines the human rights critiques developed by David Kennedy, Anne Orford and Makau Mutua, arguing that each ultimately returns to human rights as a framework with transformative possibilities. The article questions this tendency to combine criticism with renewed commitment, inviting reflection on the possibilities and limitations of reimagining human rights from within.

Title: Liberation Theology: Problematizing the Historical Projects of Democracy and Human Rights
Source/Citation: McGeoch, Graham. “Liberation Theology: Problematizing the Historical Projects of Democracy and Human Rights.” Sociedade e Cultura 23 (2020), article e59897.
Theme: Faith & Freedom of Religion; Human Rights Futures & Theory; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: McGeoch examines how Liberation Christianity and Liberation Theology have engaged with democracy and human rights in Latin America. He argues that their original emphasis on liberation risks being overshadowed by efforts to defend existing political institutions. Drawing on the idea of institutional imagination, the article considers how liberation movements might develop alternative political projects beyond established democratic and human rights frameworks.

Title: Reparations for Colonialism Beyond Legal Responsibility
Source/Citation: Ratner, Steven. “Reparations for Colonialism Beyond Legal Responsibility.” American Journal of International Law 119, no. 3 (2025): 507–529.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Ratner questions whether establishing legal responsibility should be the main focus of efforts to secure colonial reparations. He proposes a more flexible role for international law, supporting negotiations and agreements that respond to historical injustices without necessarily requiring recognition of a legal duty to compensate. The article considers how such processes could develop practical standards for future reparations arrangements.

Title: Rights of Nature in Global Perspective: Legal Pathways and Policy Implications
Source/Citation: Arreaga-Vicuña, Carmen, et al. “Rights of Nature in Global Perspective: Legal Pathways and Policy Implications.” Frontiers in Environmental Science 14 (2026), article 1647205.
Theme: Climate & Environmental Justice; Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Comparing rights-of-nature frameworks across six countries, Arreaga-Vicuña and colleagues identify constitutional, legislative and judicial approaches to recognising nature as a rights-holder. They find that legal recognition alone is insufficient without effective guardianship, access to courts and enforceable remedies. The review highlights the importance of institutional capacity, Indigenous perspectives and community participation in turning rights-of-nature principles into practice.

Title: Transforming the World with Reparations?
Source/Citation: Brunk, Ingrid, and Monica Hakimi. “Transforming the World with Reparations?” American Journal of International Law 119, no. 3 (2025): 380–396.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Economic & Development Justice; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Brunk and Hakimi distinguish between corrective reparations, which seek to remedy specific legally recognised harms, and transformative reparations, which aim to address wider inequalities rooted in historical injustice. They question whether reparations can realistically achieve such broad structural change and examine the conceptual and legal difficulties of combining these approaches. The article encourages reconsideration of what reparations can accomplish.

Title: Decolonizing Development: Reparatory Justice for People and Planet
Source/Citation: Khoday, Kishan. Decolonizing Development: Reparatory Justice for People and Planet. Expert commentary for the UNDP Development at Risk Report. United Nations Development Programme, 2025.
Theme: Economic & Development Justice; Accountability & Reparations; Climate & Environmental Justice
Key Takeaway: Khoday links contemporary environmental vulnerability in the Caribbean to the enduring effects of colonial extraction and inequality. He argues that addressing these risks requires more than financial reparations or conventional development policies. Drawing on decolonial and ecological perspectives, the paper proposes rethinking development around the interdependence of communities and ecosystems, recognising both human and non-human agency.

Title: Decolonization: The Litmus Test of the Human Rights Framework
Source/Citation: Omoigui, Isiuwa. “Decolonization: The Litmus Test of the Human Rights Framework.” The Yale Undergraduate Research Journal 2, no. 1 (2021), Article 23.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Human Rights Futures & Theory; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: Examines tensions between the individual-rights framework established after the Second World War and the collective demands of African anticolonial movements. Drawing on struggles in Algeria and Cameroon, the article questions the universalism of human rights and the authority of former colonial powers in shaping them. It considers Indigenous knowledge and practices as alternative paths towards meaningful liberation.

Title: Epistemic Violence in the Inter-American Human Rights System: Indigenous Cosmologies, Legal Pluralism and Paths Towards Decolonial Justice
Source/Citation: Carvalho de Mello, Bernardo. “Epistemic Violence in the Inter-American Human Rights System: Indigenous Cosmologies, Legal Pluralism and Paths Towards Decolonial Justice.” Third World Quarterly 47, no. 14 (2026): 2837–2860.
Theme: Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Education & Knowledge Justice; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: Carvalho de Mello examines how the Inter-American Human Rights System can marginalise Indigenous knowledge despite advances in legal recognition. Drawing on Brazilian cases and Indigenous legal philosophies, he identifies tensions between Western legal categories and relational understandings of land, nature and community. The article calls for greater recognition of Indigenous legal systems and reforms to how human rights institutions interpret evidence and administer justice.

Title: Human Rights Futures
Source/Citation: Hopgood, Stephen, Jack Snyder, and Leslie Vinjamuri, eds. Human Rights Futures. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2017.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Global Governance & International Law; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: Bringing together mainstream and critical scholars, this collection examines the achievements, limitations and possible futures of international human rights. Contributors debate what makes human rights protection effective, why progress faces resistance and whether established approaches remain adequate in a changing political landscape. The book presents competing perspectives on the conditions, strategies and institutions that may shape the future of human rights.

Title: In the Long Run: The Future as a Political Idea
Source/Citation: White, Jonathan. In the Long Run: The Future as a Political Idea. London: Profile Books, 2024.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Democracy & Political Power; Climate & Environmental Justice
Key Takeaway: White traces how changing ideas about the future have influenced political thought and democratic life. He considers how climate change, war and other crises challenge assumptions that tomorrow will bring opportunities for improvement. The book argues that maintaining a commitment to long-term political possibilities is important for democracy when uncertainty and the prospect of irreversible harm increasingly shape public life.

Title: Accountability from Below
Source/Citation: Hunt, Paul, and Anuj Kapilashrami. “Accountability from Below.” Health and Human Rights Journal 27, no. 2 (2025): 1–7.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Economic & Development Justice
Key Takeaway: Hunt and Kapilashrami question the dominance of state-centred human rights accountability and examine how communities and social movements can hold powerful actors accountable. Drawing on experiences from different regions, they propose a people-centred approach that combines grassroots organising with human rights standards. The editorial also outlines a possible independent global health accountability panel led by communities and civil society.

Title: Building a Free Internet of the Future
Source/Citation: Association for Progressive Communications. Building a Free Internet of the Future. APC, 2 June 2026.
Theme: Digital Rights & Technology; Grassroots Movements & Participation; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: This collection brings together interviews with people developing free and open digital technologies as alternatives to corporate-controlled platforms. Drawing on initiatives supported by NGI Zero, it highlights practical approaches to accessibility, privacy, information sharing and community participation. The publication shows how technological choices reflect social and political values and how communities can help shape more inclusive digital futures.

Title: Configuring the UN Human Rights System in the “Era of Implementation”: Mainland and Archipelago
Source/Citation: Hunt, Paul. “Configuring the UN Human Rights System in the ‘Era of Implementation’: Mainland and Archipelago.” Human Rights Quarterly 39, no. 3 (2017): 489–538.
Theme: Global Governance & International Law; Human Rights Futures & Theory
Key Takeaway: Hunt argues that effective human rights implementation requires engagement across the wider UN system, beyond its principal human rights institutions. He distinguishes between the traditional human rights “mainland” and an emerging “archipelago” of initiatives within specialised agencies and other UN bodies. The article proposes greater institutional ownership of human rights and new approaches to cooperation and implementation.

Title: International Organizations and the Fight for Accountability: The Remedies and Reparations Gap
Source/Citation: Ferstman, Carla. International Organizations and the Fight for Accountability: The Remedies and Reparations Gap. Oxford University Press, 2017.
Theme: Accountability & Reparations; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: Ferstman examines why international organisations often fail to provide effective remedies and reparations for violations of human rights and humanitarian law attributed to them. The book identifies legal and institutional barriers to accountability, questions justifications for limiting organisational responsibility, and argues that reparations should reflect the nature of violations and resulting harm rather than the identity of the responsible institution.

Title: Capitalism, Colonisation and the Ecocide-Genocide Nexus
Source/Citation: Crook, Martin. Capitalism, Colonisation and the Ecocide-Genocide Nexus. University of London Press, 2024.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Climate & Environmental Justice; Indigenous Rights & Knowledge
Key Takeaway: Crook examines the relationship between colonialism, capitalism and ecological destruction, focusing on Indigenous and place-based communities in Kenya and Australia. Combining political-economic analysis with original interviews, he explores how land dispossession, extractive industries and development policies can threaten communities' cultural and physical survival. The book connects historical colonial violence with contemporary environmental injustice.

Title: Gaza and the Colonial Right to Self-defence: Legal Absurdities and the Circular Reasoning of Violence
Source/Citation: Moussa, Passent, and Colin Samson. “Gaza and the Colonial Right to Self-defence: Legal Absurdities and the Circular Reasoning of Violence.” International Journal for the Semiotics of Law (2026). Published 23 June 2026.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Global Governance & International Law; Accountability & Reparations
Key Takeaway: Moussa and Samson critically examine the use of self-defence arguments in the context of Gaza, situating the violence following 7 October 2023 within a longer history of occupation and dispossession. They question how international legal doctrines can legitimise continued violence and argue that existing legal and political frameworks have failed to prevent mass atrocities and protect Palestinian rights.

Title: Hewers of Wood and Drawers of Water: English Subaltern Education from the Charity Schools to the Neoliberal Meritocracy of Widening Participation
Source/Citation: Cunningham, Christopher, and Colin Samson. “Hewers of Wood and Drawers of Water: English Subaltern Education from the Charity Schools to the Neoliberal Meritocracy of Widening Participation.” Critical Social Policy 45, no. 2 (2025).
Theme: Education & Knowledge Justice; Economic & Development Justice; Democracy & Political Power
Key Takeaway: Cunningham and Samson trace continuities between historical education programmes for working-class children and contemporary widening participation policies in English higher education. They argue that initiatives presented as expanding opportunity can also reproduce social hierarchies by preparing disadvantaged students for existing labour structures. Their analysis questions meritocratic narratives and highlights the growing financial burden placed on students seeking social mobility.

Title: The Colonialism of Human Rights: Ongoing Hypocrisies of Western Liberalism
Source/Citation: Samson, Colin. The Colonialism of Human Rights: Ongoing Hypocrisies of Western Liberalism. Polity Press, 2020.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Accountability & Reparations
Key Takeaway: Samson challenges claims of human rights universality by examining the historical relationship between Western liberalism, colonialism and slavery. Drawing on examples involving Indigenous peoples and communities affected by racial discrimination, he argues that colonial hierarchies continue to shape whose rights are recognised and protected. The book advocates reparative justice and approaches to law grounded in Indigenous experiences and perspectives.

Title: Take Back the City: Grassroots Struggles, Housing Justice, and Decolonial Futures in Belfast
Source/Citation: Urban Political Podcast. “Take Back the City: Grassroots Struggles, Housing Justice, and Decolonial Futures in Belfast.” Episode 110, 25 June 2026.
Theme: Grassroots Movements & Participation; Economic & Development Justice; Decolonisation & Colonial Justice
Key Takeaway: This episode examines grassroots struggles for housing justice and the right to the city in Belfast. Drawing on community organising and anti-colonial perspectives, contributors discuss how segregation, land governance and structural inequality shape urban life. They explore solidarity, mutual aid and collective stewardship as practical approaches to building more inclusive and equitable urban futures.

Title: FORGE 2023: Future of Rights and Governance
Source/Citation: OpenGlobalRights. FORGE 2023. Video collection from the Future of Rights and Governance inaugural conference, New York, 3–5 November 2023.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Indigenous Rights & Knowledge; Global Governance & International Law
Key Takeaway: This collection brings together presentations exploring the future of human rights and global governance. Speakers address Indigenous knowledge, ecological justice, democracy, political imagination and institutional transformation. Through academic discussions, activist perspectives and artistic performances, the videos consider how human rights thinking and practice might evolve in response to contemporary crises and emerging challenges.

Title: Future Perfect | Futur Antérieur
Source/Citation: African Futures Lab. Future Perfect | Futur Antérieur. Podcast series hosted by Liliane Umubyeyi and Amah Edoh.
Theme: Decolonisation & Colonial Justice; Accountability & Reparations; Gender & Social Justice
Key Takeaway: This podcast brings together activists, scholars and artists to examine historical and contemporary forms of racial injustice across Africa, Europe and the Americas. Through conversations on colonial legacies, reparations, economic inequalities and collective resistance, it highlights different approaches to challenging structural injustice and explores possibilities for more equitable futures.

Title: The Past, Present and Future of the Human Rights Movement
Source/Citation: Open Society Foundations. The Past, Present and Future of the Human Rights Movement. Online panel discussion moderated by James A. Goldston, 8 October 2026.
Theme: Human Rights Futures & Theory; Democracy & Political Power; Grassroots Movements & Participation
Key Takeaway: This discussion reflects on the human rights movement's historical achievements, institutional limitations and future challenges. Panellists examine the influence of colonialism, geopolitical power and grassroots struggles on human rights advocacy. They debate how the movement can respond to contemporary crises, address structural inequalities and strengthen its independence, political relevance and connection with affected communities.
